items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Only 1.5 percent of human DNA codes for proteins
items.claim: The human genome has about 3 billion base pairs. Of these, only about 1.5 percent — 45 million bases — encode proteins. The rest was once called 'junk DNA'. Most of it isn't.
items.prompt: What does the non-coding majority actually do?

options.text: It's all junk left over from evolution

It includes promoters, enhancers, insulators, microRNA genes, long non-coding RNAs, ribosomal RNA, structural sequences, transposable elements (some still active), and regions whose function is still being mapped
It codes for proteins we haven't found
It's only present in cells that have stopped dividing

items.reveal_title: ENCODE and the redefinition of junk
items.reveal:
The ENCODE Project (2012) reported biochemical activity (transcription, transcription-factor binding, chromatin features) in about 80 percent of the genome. Whether all of this counts as 'function' was hotly debated.

Certain categories of non-coding DNA have clear roles:
- Promoters/enhancers: regulate gene expression in time and place. Disrupting them causes disease (e.g., enhancer mutations causing limb deformity).
- microRNAs: ~22-nucleotide RNAs that tune protein levels.
- Long non-coding RNAs: XIST silences a whole X chromosome in females.
- Transposable elements: about 45 percent of the genome; some still mobile.

Much DNA may also be 'spacer' or accumulated parasitic sequence with no current function — but the cell is full of layers of regulation built from non-coding DNA.
items.why: Genome size was thought to scale with organism complexity. Onions have 5 times more DNA than humans. Most DNA isn't there to encode proteins — and may be doing many things at once.

items.title: Species are vanishing 100 to 1000 times faster than normal
items.claim: The fossil record gives a 'background' extinction rate: roughly 1 species per million per year. Current rates are 100 to 1000 times that — and rising. Many biologists call it the sixth mass extinction.

options.text: Asteroid impact like 66 million years ago
Habitat destruction (especially tropical deforestation), invasive species, climate change, pollution and overharvesting — a multi-cause anthropogenic mass extinction with no single dominant mechanism

items.reveal:
The five previous mass extinctions (Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous) each saw 50-95% of species disappear over geological timescales. The Permian was the worst — ~96% of marine species lost over ~60,000 years.

The current rate, calculated from documented vertebrate extinctions (Ceballos, Ehrlich and others), is 100-1000 times background. Insect biomass declines (Hallmann et al. 2017, Krefeld study) show 75% reductions over 27 years in German nature reserves.

Human impacts: forest cover reduced by ~30% globally since 1700; ocean fish biomass down ~50% since 1970; freshwater vertebrates down 84% (WWF Living Planet Report). Climate change adds an accelerating layer.

Protected areas and conservation work — by some measures, extinction rates would have been 4x higher without them.

Mass extinctions reshape evolution for tens of millions of years. We won't return to the world we know within human-relevant timeframes — the species we lose are lost.
items.why: Species loss feels gradual. The rate is geological in magnitude — comparable to events that left fossil-record-defining boundaries. We are living through one.
